issues.description: Predicate reads awkwardly; extract a named helper like isLayerStatement(node) to express intent directly.
issues.detail: `!(nodeName === 'layer' && typeof node.nodes === 'undefined')` buries the rule behind a negation. The data distinction is: a bare `@layer foo;` statement is allowed before `@import`; `@layer foo {}` with a block is not. A named helper or short comment would make the invariant self-evident at the call site.

PostCSS represents block-less at-rules with `nodes` absent and block-having ones with an array — a documented structural property, not a possibly-undeclared identifier. A direct null/undefined check is shorter, matches surrounding codebase idioms, and expresses the data shape plainly. `typeof` is defensive verbiage with no payoff here.

issues.description: Add a paired accept-case test for the statement form `@layer foo;` before `@import`.
issues.detail: The new reject test covers `@layer foo {}` before `@import`, but no test asserts the still-allowed `@layer foo;` statement form. Adding one accept-case pins down the distinction the predicate encodes and guards against a future refactor silently flipping the condition. Cheap to add; makes the invariant testable in both directions.

synthesis.summary: Unanimous panel verdict: the patch is small, correct, and right-sized. It encodes the CSS Cascade rule that a bare `@layer foo;` statement is allowed before `@import` while `@layer foo {}` with a block is not. All three reviewers converge on the same polish notes: the negated inline predicate would read better as a named helper, `typeof === 'undefined'` should be a direct null/undefined check matching codebase idioms, and the test suite should pin the still-allowed statement form alongside the new reject case. Accept after trivial fixup.
